issues.title: Huge-page backed hash-join pointer table for large builds
issues.hypothesis: Large in-memory HJ builds cost ~100-200ns per build row, and more than half of that is not the input scan. Build-only micro (hot, 8 threads; lineitem 1995 = 9.1M build rows, 0 probe rows, forced with SET disabled_optimizers='join_order,build_side_probe_side'): HJ query 1.34s user + 0.42s SYS vs 0.40s user / 0 sys for the bare scan. That leaves about 0.95s user, ~104ns per row, plus 0.4s of kernel time. BF fill is only ~0.1s of it (join_filter_pushdown off: 1.21-1.24s). In hot q07 the middle HJ builds 1.46M lineitem rows and probes 100K orders: 0.287s CPU (~196ns per build row). q09's o_orderkey HJ (3.27M build) takes 0.80s and q03's (1.45M build) 0.38s. E0037 showed that partition-local slots do not shrink the working set. The pointer table is NextPowerOfTwo(count*2) 8-byte entries (join_hashtable.hpp:417): 32MB for 1.45M rows and 256MB for 9.1M. It comes from buffer_manager.GetBufferAllocator().Allocate (join_hashtable.cpp:804/812). jemalloc runs with oversize_threshold 256MB, so the biggest tables are fresh mmaps every query, and the faults and zeroing show up as sys time. Each insert in InsertHashes and each probe in GetRowPointers touches a random 8-byte slot. With 4KB pages a 32-256MB table covers 8K-65K pages, far beyond the L2 TLB (~1.5K entries), so nearly every slot access is a TLB miss plus a page walk on top of the cache miss. With 2MB pages the same table is 16-128 pages, so walks mostly disappear and faults drop 512x.
issues.plan: Step 0 (cheap gate): Read /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled and defrag. If enabled is [never], abandon. If [always], the table may already be THP-backed: then check whether the allocation is 2MB-aligned and whether jemalloc's opt_thp or the decay settings defeat it, and measure before coding. Step 1: In src/execution/join_hashtable.cpp JoinHashTable::AllocatePointerTable, when capacity*sizeof(ht_entry_t) >= 4MB (Linux only, #ifdef __linux__), allocate the table so that it is 2MB-aligned and call madvise(ptr, size, MADV_HUGEPAGE) before the first touch. The first touch is InitializePointerTable's std::fill_n, which runs in the parallel finalize tasks. Simplest way: over-allocate by 2MB through the same BufferAllocator (memory accounting unchanged), keep the AllocatedData, and set `entries` to the 2MB-aligned address inside it. Keep hash_map.GetSize() consistent, or keep the usable capacity in a separate member: the reuse branch at :801 divides GetSize() by the entry size and the D_ASSERT at :815 compares sizes, so both need adjusting. Alternatively add a small helper next to the block_allocator.cpp madvise code (src/storage/block_allocator.cpp:72-77) that mmaps 2MB-aligned memory with MADV_HUGEPAGE, freed by munmap through a custom PrivateAllocatorData. Step 2: rerun the build-only micro above, the q07 query and q09, and compare user and sys time with the madvise on and off (a temporary env var or setting is fine during testing; remove it before landing). Optionally apply the same helper to the GroupedAggregateHashTable entries array only if it is the same few lines; otherwise leave it for a follow-up.
issues.expected_gain: HJ build and probe CPU on large builds -20..-40% when TLB misses dominate: q09 (0.80s HJ), q07 (0.29s), q03 (0.38s), q05/q08 (similar lineitem-orders joins), q18 outer joins. Roughly -3..-6% geomean if the TLB hypothesis holds; also removes ~0.4s sys per 9M-row build.
issues.generality: Every hash join with more than ~250K build rows (pointer table >= 4MB) on Linux, which is every big fact-to-fact or fact-to-dimension join. Small joins are unchanged, below the threshold. Possible slowdowns: THP compaction stalls when memory is fragmented (defrag setting), and an extra 2MB of slack per large table.
issues.risk: Low-medium. The change is contained to allocation, with no change to hashing semantics. The risks are pointer-alignment bookkeeping with the reuse path in AllocatePointerTable and environment dependence on the THP mode (step 0 gates it). Gain may be small if the kernel already backs these mappings with THP.
